sections.html:
Whether you list with an agent, sell on your own or accept an as-is cash offer, a Stafford sale ends at the same municipal checkpoint: a resale Certificate of Occupancy for an existing structure from the township's Office of Inspection. Under Chapter 81 of the Stafford code, a house that changes occupancy needs an inspection by the Code Official, after which a continuing certificate of occupancy is issued.

You submit the Application for Existing Structure Certificate of Occupancy and can reach the office at 609-597-1000, extension 8532. The township describes the review as visual only, not a structural investigation, so a buyer will still want a private home inspection.

Stafford sits on the Jersey Shore in southern Ocean County, and many owners have been in their homes a long time. The estimated population is 30,958 as of July 2025, up 8.2 percent from April 2020. Of 12,007 households, 90.3 percent own, the middle home value is $426,200 and median household income is $117,612. Residents 65 and older make up 22.0 percent. Median gross rent is $1,800.

Many houses date from the 1950s to the 1980s, and some are converted summer homes. Heating systems and electrical panels are where the township inspector tends to look closely.

sections.h2: Paperwork that goes with the application
sections.html:
Supporting items for the Stafford certificate
DocumentWhen you need it
Notarized Heat CertificationAlways. The seller or agent confirms a professional inspected the heating system and any solid-fuel burner. Clerical staff can notarize it at the counter.
Letter from the Stafford Municipal Utility AuthorityWhen the house is connected to public water and sewer
Water test approved by the Ocean County Health DepartmentWhen the house has a private well. The test comes from a well driller or tester.

The township's list of common violations works as a pre-listing checklist. Walk the house with it before you apply.

  • Missing outlet plates and uncovered junction boxes
  • Open spaces in an electrical panel and unsecured fixtures
  • Leaking pipes, and relief valves not piped to within 6 inches of the floor
  • Metal dryer vents, chimney caps, and house numbers at least 3 inches high
  • Handrails on stairs with more than 3 risers, and guardrails where a deck or stair is 30 inches or more above grade
  • Smoke detectors within 10 feet of sleeping areas and on every floor including the basement
  • Carbon monoxide detectors in one- and two-family homes with fuel-burning appliances or an attached garage

The township posts more on its rentals and resales page. Small fixes made before the visit save a second trip and keep the certificate on schedule.

The Heat Certification is the item sellers most often leave to the last minute. A professional has to inspect the heating system, and any fireplace, wood stove or other solid-fuel burner, before the seller or agent signs the statement. Book that visit as soon as you decide to sell, since a tradesperson's calendar can run longer than the township's.

Once the professional has finished, bring the statement to the counter. Staff can notarize it there, which saves a separate trip to a notary. Keep a copy, because your attorney and the buyer's lender may each ask for one.

Older houses in Stafford, especially converted seasonal cottages, may have had heating added piece by piece over the years. If you know of an old burner that no longer works, say so to the professional and fix or remove it rather than leaving it for the inspector to question.

Stafford is the mainland gateway to Long Beach Island. Route 72 is the only road onto the island and crosses Barnegat Bay on the Manahawkin Bay Bridge into Ship Bottom. The Garden State Parkway meets Route 72 at Exit 63. The main areas are Manahawkin around Route 9 and Route 72, Beach Haven West, Ocean Acres, Warren Grove, and smaller places such as Mayetta. The ZIP code for Manahawkin is 08050.

Stafford's house raising page refers to the Base Flood Elevation regulations and to the storm of October 27, 2012, and it describes two permit routes. In the first, the owner raises the home under a construction permit and does not reoccupy it until a Certificate of Occupancy is issued. In the second, the owner repairs the home to safe living conditions first, receives a Temporary Certificate of Occupancy, and raises it later.

Either route needs a zoning permit with a survey showing setbacks and structure height, engineered plans for the new foundation, and releases from every utility serving the building. Insurance Increased Cost of Compliance payments are tied to the permit and the final certificate.

A seller with a raised house should keep the permit, the engineering sign-off and the final certificate in one folder for the buyer's lender. A seller near the bay should ask the Zoning office which flood zone and base flood elevation apply to the address.

Shore properties often have a rental history. The township's seasonal rental page lists a $100 fee plus $50 for a reinspection. The applicant also supplies proof of paid property taxes, proof of water and sewer payment, and a floor-by-floor drawing. Long-term rentals built before 1978 need lead-based paint inspections.

If you are selling a house that has been rented, give the buyer the tax and utility proofs, the drawing and any lead inspection record.

The seller owes New Jersey's Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded, calculated from the price in the deed. Many shore owners live elsewhere, and a seller who is not a New Jersey resident must prepay estimated Gross Income Tax at closing, never less than 2% of the sale price, unless a listed exception applies. Your closing attorney will complete the forms.

1. Pick up the Application for Existing Structure Certificate of Occupancy from the Office of Inspection.
  2. Order the heating system inspection and get the Heat Certification notarized.
  3. Request the utility authority letter, or arrange the well water test.
  4. Walk the house against the violations list and fix what you find.
  5. Pass the visual inspection and collect the certificate for your attorney.

A cash buyer who takes the house as it is can still ask you to complete these steps. Ask early whether the buyer will take them over.

faqs.q: Does Stafford require an inspection when a house is sold?
faqs.a: Yes. Chapter 81 of the Stafford code calls for an inspection by the Code Official on every change of occupancy, followed by a continuing certificate of occupancy. Apply with the Existing Structure Certificate of Occupancy form.

It is a notarized statement from the seller or the seller's agent that a professional inspected the heating system and any fireplace, wood stove or other solid-fuel burner. Clerical staff can notarize it at the counter.

faqs.q: How is a private well handled in a Stafford sale?
faqs.a: The well water must be tested by a well driller or tester and approved by the Ocean County Health Department. That approval takes the place of the utility letter that houses on public water and sewer provide.

faqs.q: Is the Stafford inspection a full home inspection?
faqs.a: No. The township calls its review visual only and says a complete overview of the property comes from a registered home inspection agency. Buyers usually order their own inspection as well.

faqs.q: What does a Stafford seasonal rental license cost?
faqs.a: The fee is $100, plus $50 for a reinspection. The applicant also supplies proof of paid property taxes, proof of water and sewer payment, and a floor-by-floor drawing.
